title: ‘These last till tomorrow’: the refusal
theme: Naciketas, unmoved, answers the temptations: such pleasures are uncertain of tomorrow and wear out the senses; all life, however long, is short; Death may keep his chariots, his dancing and song.

words.context: Śaṅkara: «श्वो भविष्यन्ति न वेति सन्दिह्यमान एव येषां भावो»

sandhi.rule: āḥ drops its visarga before the voiced m, P. 8.3.17 (भोभगोअघोअपूर्वस्य योऽशि) and P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य).
yat before a vowel becomes yad, P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते). antaka + etat: a + e give ai, P. 6.1.88 (वृद्धिरेचि).
tava + eva give tavaiva, P. 6.1.88 (वृद्धिरेचि). vāhāḥ before t becomes vāhās, P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः).

samasa.vigraha: श्वो भविष्यन्ति न वेति सन्दिह्यमान एव येषां भावो
samasa.meaning: whose being is uncertain tomorrow; the vigraha is Śaṅkara’s. Raṅgarāmānuja divides śvo ’bhāvāḥ instead (see ambiguities)

morphology.note: Causative of jṝ ‘grow old’: ‘make old, wear out’ (Śaṅkara: «अपक्षपयन्ति»).

translation.literal: [Things] of tomorrow’s existence, O Ender; what [is] the vigour of all the senses of a mortal, this they wear out. Even all life [is] short indeed. Yours alone [be] the chariots; yours the dancing and singing.
translation.readable: These things last only till tomorrow, Death, and they wear away the strength of every sense a mortal has. Even the longest life is short. Keep your chariots; keep your dancing and your song.

anvaya: अन्तक, [एते] श्वोभावाः । मर्त्यस्य सर्वेन्द्रियाणाम् यत् एतत् तेजः [तत् ते] जरयन्ति । सर्वम् अपि जीवितम् अल्पम् एव । वाहाः तव एव [सन्तु], नृत्यगीते तव [स्ताम्] ।
syntax: Short nominal sentences. The first is a single predicate (śvobhāvāḥ) whose subject — the pleasures offered — is understood; the second uses a relative (yat … etat) for the object of jarayanti; the last two leave the verb ‘be’ to be supplied (tavaiva vāhāḥ, tava nṛtyagīte).

ambiguities.note: The letters allow two divisions. Śaṅkara reads one word, ‘whose being is doubtful tomorrow’: «श्वो भविष्यन्ति न वेति सन्दिह्यमान एव येषां भावो भवनं». Raṅgarāmānuja divides śvaḥ abhāvāḥ, ‘whose non-being is tomorrow’ — «श्वः अभावः येषां ते तथोक्ताः» — that is, they will not last two days. Madhva’s text writes the avagraha (श्वोऽभावा). The sense is the same.
Śaṅkara construes yad etat with tejaḥ: ‘this vigour of all the senses’, which the pleasures wear out.

beginner: Death has offered the boy everything. Now Naciketas answers, calmly. These things, he says, are not sure to be there tomorrow. While they last they wear down the strength of all the senses. And even the longest life is short, so long life is no great gift either. Keep your horses and chariots, and your dancing and singing; they are yours. Śaṅkara says the boy stood unshaken like a deep lake. He also notes that even the life of Brahmā, the longest of all, is short. The boy is not refusing pleasure out of fear; he has simply seen through it.
analogy: Like a traveller offered a beautifully furnished room in a house that will be pulled down tomorrow.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: That the things offered last only till tomorrow and wear out the senses, that all life is short, and that Death may keep his chariots, dancing and song.

commentary.q: How does the boy hear the temptation?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: tempted thus by Death, Naciketas speaks unshaken, like a great lake — «मृत्युना एवं प्रलोभ्यमानोऽपि नचिकेता महाह्रदवदक्षोभ्य आह». Such pleasures are harmful because they waste virtue, strength, wisdom, vigour and fame — «धर्मवीर्यप्रज्ञातेजोयशःप्रभृतीनां क्षपयितृत्वात्». And all life, even Brahmā’s, is short: «सर्वं यद्ब्रह्मणोऽपि जीवितम् आयुः अल्पमेव».

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: Śaṅkara reads śvobhāvāḥ as one compound (‘whose being is doubtful tomorrow’); Raṅgarāmānuja divides śvo ’bhāvāḥ, ‘whose non-existence comes tomorrow’ — «श्वः अभावः येषां ते तथोक्ताः», «दिनद्वयस्थायिनो न भवन्ति इत्यर्थः». Both make the pleasures transient.

advaita.text: The pleasures are transient and harmful, wasting the vigour of the senses and of virtue; and even the longest life is short: «सर्वं यद्ब्रह्मणोऽपि जीवितम् आयुः अल्पमेव».

visistadvaita.text: The same reading: the pleasures do not last two days, and even Brahmā’s life is short, much more ours — «ब्रह्मणोऽपि जीवितं स्वल्पम्, किमुत अस्मदादिजीवितम्» — so long life is not worth choosing either.

schools.disagreement: No disagreement of substance; they divide the first word differently. Madhva’s bhāṣya on the passage 1.1.26–29 comments only on ‘the great passing-on’ of 1.1.29.

parallels.note: The Gītā: even the worlds up to Brahmā’s are subject to return; Śaṅkara’s gloss, that even Brahmā’s life is short, makes the same point.

contemporary.text: Things that wear out the one who enjoys them are poor bargains, however bright. The boy’s answer is not puritanism but arithmetic: what lasts till tomorrow cannot answer a question about what lasts. This is a reflection, not a claim made by the text.

reflect.beginner: Which of the things you enjoy most will still be with you in ten years?
reflect.deeper: Is a pleasure less valuable because it does not last? What else would make it valuable?
reflect.practice: Notice one thing today that leaves you more tired than it found you, and one that leaves you clearer.

flags.note: Madhva’s text reads nṛttagītam for nṛtyagīte (corrections.json).
śvobhāvāḥ (Śaṅkara) or śvo ’bhāvāḥ (Raṅgarāmānuja; Madhva’s text writes the avagraha).
